title: Europe joins global stock market rally as AI trade rebounds - as it happened
byline: Lauren Almeida, Phillip Inman, Mark Sweney
excerpt: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

17h ago

Closing post

Time to wrap up…

Almost all pensions and benefits systems in the UK are unavailable after a “cyber incident”.

Anyone trying to check their state pension, make an application for disability benefits or claim universal credit was not able to do so on Friday morning.

Regular benefits and pensions payments are not affected and would continue to be made as normal, the Department for Work and Pension said.

But there were reports from members of the public who said payments they had expected to be in their account had not arrived on Friday morning.

The cause of the incident, and whether it is the result of a cyber-attack, is not publicly known but the department is working with the National Cyber Security Centre.

You can follow our coverage of the cyber incident here:

The governor of the Bank of England has said he fears banks could attempt to pass on the £1.5bn cost of Labour’s tax increase on their profits.

The chancellor, John Healey, used his first budget last month to temporarily increase the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% to 6% for a 15-month period from January, with the proceeds funding “breathing space” to relieve pressure on household finances.

While the level of the increase was less than banks had feared – there had been wide speculation that Healey would reinstate the 8% tax level that was in place until 2023 – the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, said he would not be surprised if banks attempted to pass the costs on to customers to “protect their earnings”.

An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.

The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

London-based TrueLayer, which enables payments to be made between bank accounts without using cards, said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for an order for a real customer.

US stocks rise as AI trade rebounds

Wall Street has opened higher today, with the S&P 500 rising by 1.1% at the open while the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.6%.

Shares in the memory company SanDisk are up 6.5%, while Micron and Marvell Technology are both up by about 3%.

US futures are pointing to a strong rise at the open in New York – futures for the S&P 500 are up 1.64%, while the Nasdaq is poised for a 2.3% rise.

Norse Atlantic Airways declares bankruptcy

Norse Atlantic Airways has declared bankruptcy, the long-haul budget carrier said on Friday.

The Norwegian airline, which operates long-haul flights around the world including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia, warned yesterday it would have to file for bankruptcy unless it was able to secure short-term financing.

The airline, like many worldwide, is reeling from surging jet fuel prices since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, as well as hitting consumer confidence.

Norse CEO Eivind Roald in a statement:

The board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution.

We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers,
employees and partners. The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations.”

Norse was founded in 2021 as it sought to step into the space vacated by Norwegian Air, whose attempts to fly budget long-haul were also abandoned as unviable.

The Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has warned that banks operating in the UK – those that must pay the government’s higher bank levy – could pass on the cost to customers. This could be in the form of costlier mortgage products or higher business loan rates.

Some analysts are sceptical.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell said, it would “not be the biggest surprise in the world” if the banks tried to pass on the costs of the bank tax in higher loan charges, especially when challenger banks trying to enter the mortgage market are still finding it relative hard to make a decisive breakthrough.

However, he said competition was an obstacle.

Nationwide’s 1% deposit, six times salary mortgage shows there is some scope for consumers to shop around.”

The Bank’s decision to ease capital regulatory requirements, despite warning of higher risks at the same time, also gives the banks a chance to add to their loan books and recoup some of the additional levy that way, should they so choose.”

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, said:

While the banks themselves have stated that higher taxes will lead to increased costs for consumers, the stock market is telling us a different story. The UK’s incumbent banks have seen their stock prices fall sharply in the past month, since the surcharge increase was announced. Lloyds is down 8%, and NatWest is lower by 10%, this suggests the market may expect banks to absorb the tax rise, which challenges their profitability in the future.

One thing that could stop banks from passing on the effect of the increase is that the surcharge is time limited, and is legislated to fall back to 3% in April 2028. If banks are confident that the next budget won’t see an extension of the extended surcharge, then banks may be willing to absorb the cost for one year.”

US stock market set to join global rally as AI trade returns

It looks like it will be a strong open later in the US market – futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 are up 2.7% as optimism around the AI trade returns.

Shares in the memory company SanDisk are up 11% in pre-market trading. Nvidia is up 4%, while Micron and Marvell Technology are both up by about 7% in pre-market.

In Europe, the Sotxx Europe 600 is now up 1%, driven by a 2% gain its tech sector. The Austrian circuit board manufacturer AT&S is the best performer on the continent, with its shares up 7%.

The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 is up 0.8%, led by a rally in its miner stocks.

French economy shrinks 0.2% in third quarter

France’s economic output shrank by -0.2% in the third quarter, compared with a previous estimate of -0.1%.

The French statistics agency found that its economy was hit by a drop in investment in the construction sector and a fall in exports.

Charlotte de Montpellier, a senior economist at the bank ING, said that the figures show that the French economy has now contracted for three consecutive quarters.

Following this revision, the annual growth carry-over for 2026 stands at only 0.1%. It is very difficult to see domestic demand rebounding strongly enough in the fourth quarter to improve this result.

Business and consumer confidence both deteriorated in October and November. A weakening labour market and growing fears of unemployment will keep households cautious. At the same time, weak demand and a lack of visibility will continue to weigh on business investment.

She added that the bank now expects zero growth in the final quarter of the year and that France will enter 2027 “without economic momentum”.

This would leave average GDP growth at just 0.1% in 2026, well below the 1.0% we expect for the eurozone.

The outlook for 2027 remains very gloomy. Salaried employment fell by 94,400 jobs over the past year, a decline of 0.3%. The situation is even worse in the private sector, where 109,000 jobs were lost over the same period, a fall of 0.5%.

The weakening labour market will increasingly weigh on household confidence, income and consumption. Financing conditions also remain difficult, while uncertainty over future taxes and public spending is exceptionally high. Both businesses and households are likely to keep postponing some projects.

It is therefore difficult to identify a driver capable of generating a meaningful recovery in domestic demand over the next few quarters. The third-quarter contraction and the likely absence of a fourth-quarter rebound also leave a very weak starting point for 2027. France will enter next year without economic momentum. Even if quarterly growth turns slightly positive again, this will not be enough to produce solid annual growth. We expect GDP to grow by just 0.4% on average in 2027, with risks still tilted to the downside.

Pizza history: AI agent’s cardless purchase is a first for UK

Mark Sweney

An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK made with an AI agent using cardless payment technology.

The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

London-based TrueLayer, which enables payments to be made between bank accounts without using cards, said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for an order for a real customer.

The TrueLayer chief executive, Francesco Simoneschi, said in an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme:

We completed this payment transaction with Papa John’s with no account numbers, no password [and] handled with the highest possible security profile.

We talked with the AI agent, described the occasion and dietary requirements. Of course the agent suggested different flavours and quantities. We confirmed the order and the pizza arrived later.”

More on the “cyber incident” at the Department for Work and Pensions – while DWP says pension and benefit payments are carrying on as usual, the online services that have been taken down as a precaution include:

  • Tell Us Once service ( a service that lets you report a death to most government organisations in one go)

  • Pension credit calculator

  • Universal credit

Reported problems on the government website started to roll in on Thursday night, according to the tracking platform Downdetector.

It is not clear yet what the nature of the cyber incident is, or if there have been any data breaches. But DWP is advising that it will never message people to ask them for bank details or ask them to click on links.

A DWP spokesperson said:

We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution following a cyber incident.

We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible to minimise any disruption.

Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal.

Shares in Japan Tobacco are up 4.5% today after reports emerged that the company and its US peer Altria are considering a takeover of the UK cigarette maker Imperial Brands.

Imperial Brands shares have nudged up 0.4% this morning, after rising up by as much as 18% yesterday.

Altria, whose Philip Morris division makes Marlboro and Benson & Hedges cigarettes, told the City on Thursday that it was considering an offer. If made it was likely to be solely in cash, it said.

Imperial Brands told investors yesterday that it had not received an offer yet but would consider any proposals.

Imperial makes a range of cigarettes including JPS, Davidoff, Gauloises and Lambert & Butler, Golden Virginia rolling tobacco, Rizla rolling papers and the Blu vaping brand.

A takeover of the £25.8bn company would mark one of the biggest acquisitions on the FTSE 100 in recent history and add to a long string of companies leaving the UK market.

Europe joins global stock market rally

European stocks are rising this morning, joining a broader global market rally as some of the optimism around the AI trade returns.

The UK’s FTSE 100 is up 0.7%. The Stoxx Europe 600 is up 0.9%, led by a 2% rise in its tech sector.

Asian stock markets also rallied strongly overnight, with the Japanese Nikkei up 2% and the South Korean Kospi – which relies heavily on chip makers Samsung Electronics and SKHynix – rose by 4.3%.

In China, the CSI 300 shot up 4% after Beijing promised to strengthen the role of its state-backed “national team” (state-backed investors) in helping stabilise the market.

Futures for US stocks are also pointing to a rise when the market there opens this afternoon – albeit for a shorter trading session the day after Thanksgiving.

Kathleen Brooks, of the broker XTB, notes however that the US tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 is currently down 10% over the course of the past four weeks.

The Nasdaq briefly touched bear market territory on Wednesday after declining 20% from its October peak, however, it staged a significant turnaround rally, which may be extended later today.

The recovery in stocks seems technical, it is fairly typical for a recovery after a large drop in just a few months. Over $20 trillion in value has been knocked off stocks, mostly tech, in the past two months. Investors panicked about the AI trade, which triggered stock market disruption.

However, while technical indicators suggest that a recovery could be on the cards, the fundamental problems surrounding the AI trade remain. The questions that caused the market panic are still unanswered, for example, concerns about the profitability of the AI trade and financing costs, but for now these are on the backburner.

Government takes some work and pensions services offline after "cyber incident"

The UK’s Department for Work and Pensions has taken some of its services offline after a “cyber incident”.

The government department said it was a “precaution” after it identified a cyber incident affecting its systems. It said regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal.

It said in a statement:

We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption.

…If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links.

Bailey has also warned around the growing power of artificial intelligence models.

He told Politico that lawmakers, not regulators, will need to set the guardrails for the technology.

He said:

It’s a bit like rearing children. You have to give them the chance to do things, but you also have to set some sort of boundaries as it were.

…The public needs to trust this technology. There needs to be greater transparency, explanation of what the things do, how they do it, what we’re doing.

It’s sensible to come at it from that angle and say, we’ve got to have stronger government understanding, stronger government coordination on this stuff. Regulation may follow it.”

Yesterday Bailey told a press conference that policymakers were worried about “open weight” AI – open source models, many of which are being developed in China.

The Bank also raised fears for the first time about emerging quantum computing capabilities potentially undermining the encryption technology that protects essential financial transactions.

Bailey emphasised that it was crucial, and possible, for banks to start to build up their defences against quantum risks, even while the technology was in nascent development. He said:

It could have powers that go beyond what we’re seeing with frontier AI and have substantial power to undermine cryptography.

Yesterday the Bank’s deputy governor for financial stability, Sarah Breeden, said it was important to keep in mind that households would “face this [mortgage] shock with strong balance sheets”.

She said household debt was relatively low, at a level last seen in the early 2000s.

So they start from a position of some resilience. And secondly … while there’s a distributional effect and some households would be hit more than others, in aggregate we think this is absorbable.”

UK's bank tax hike could hit borrowers and savers, BoE governor warns

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Some rather gloomy news to start Friday as Andrew Bailey, the governor of the Bank of England, has warned that British banks will probably try to pass on the cost of higher taxes to their customers.

Last month the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans to double the bank surcharge, which is levied on top of corporation tax, to 6% from January. He said the increase – expected to be worth £1.5bn – would be “time-limited”, lasting 15 months, in order “to pay for immediate support on energy bills”.

But Bailey has told the Times that he would not be surprised if banks attempted to pass on higher levies so they could “protect their earnings”.

He said:

It’s a market economy, so these are decisions banks will have to take. You could understand that they will look to pass it on because they will be targeting a rate of return.

Now, how successful they will be depends on all sorts of things: market conditions, competition within the industry and so on. It wouldn’t be surprising to find out that they will start by trying to do that.

Several analysts have predicted that banks will try to offset their higher tax bills by charging higher interest rates on loans or offering less generous saving rates.

Bailey’s comments came as the Bank’s latest report found that more than 400,000 UK homeowners will face a £500-a-month increase in their mortgage payments over the next three years, as rising interest rates heap extra pressure on households.

It found that out of the 7 million borrowers coming off fixed-rate deals before December 2029, about 6.5 million would have to cough up extra funds to cover their home loan payments.

Warnings about the increases came after policymakers at the Bank of England hiked interest rates from 3.75% to 4% this month. The Bank also hinted at another increase in interest rates to combat inflationary pressure caused by the Iran war. The financial markets have predicted three quarter-point rate rises by summer 2027.

Meanwhile energy bills are also rising – this week the energy regulator for Great Britain raised the cap on household energy bills by 26%, starting from January.

  • Second day of EU council summit

  • US stock market closes early today at 1pm Eastern time

Almost all pensions and benefits systems in the UK are unavailable after a “cyber incident”.

Anyone trying to check their state pension, make an application for disability benefits or claim universal credit was not able to do so on Friday morning.

Regular benefits and pensions payments are not affected and would continue to be made as normal, the Department for Work and Pension said.

But there were reports from members of the public who said payments they had expected to be in their account had not arrived on Friday morning.

The cause of the incident, and whether it is the result of a cyber-attack, is not publicly known but the department is working with the National Cyber Security Centre.

The governor of the Bank of England has said he fears banks could attempt to pass on the £1.5bn cost of Labour’s tax increase on their profits.

The chancellor, John Healey, used his first budget last month to temporarily increase the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% to 6% for a 15-month period from January, with the proceeds funding “breathing space” to relieve pressure on household finances.

While the level of the increase was less than banks had feared – there had been wide speculation that Healey would reinstate the 8% tax level that was in place until 2023 – the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, said he would not be surprised if banks attempted to pass the costs on to customers to “protect their earnings”.

An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.

The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

London-based TrueLayer, which enables payments to be made between bank accounts without using cards, said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for an order for a real customer.

Norse Atlantic Airways has declared bankruptcy, the long-haul budget carrier said on Friday.

The Norwegian airline, which operates long-haul flights around the world including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia, warned yesterday it would have to file for bankruptcy unless it was able to secure short-term financing.
